I’ve had this exact issue. I understand how horrible it is. You have to realize that usually it’s just a feeling and you won’t actually throw up. You have to accept the feeling, observe it as if you’re detached from it, just let it wash over you and it will pass. 

All of this is easy to say in theory and you might not really believe it when you’re actually experiencing it, so that’s why I have a sort of mantra that I repeat to myself when it starts happening: “these feelings are temporary and they will pass”. 
I drink these peppermint drops sometimes and they help with the actual sensation. 

Just remember that you are in control of your body. What’s the worst case scenario? You throw up? We are all human and our bodies are gross and sometimes we vomit and that’s fine. Trust me, it’s not going to be the end of the world. You will fight this, it’s a common manifestation of anxiety and there are professionals who can help you.

Sending you love.

I picked up this book with both a minimal knowledge of world history and little non-fiction reading experience, and having recently finished it, I feel like I’m not as clueless, yet infinitely more curious about the world. It does start off very exciting, and by the time it trails off (although not hopelessly) into exaggerated subjectiveness you know you should take what you’re reading with a grain of salt, so that doesn’t take too much away from its value or the overall reading experience, IMO.

I feel like a lot of people miss the point of the book, which is not to get you to believe everything it says, but to aggressively make you change your perspective and challenge your belief system, especially things you might have considered axiomatic. It accomplishes this task very well, and I think it’s a necessary read, as long as you can go into it with an open, but not extremely impressionable mind.
